C001.subject: Intermittent fasting
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting long-term weight loss]

qualifier.description: While some trials show short-term weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction, sustained weight loss beyond 12 months remains poorly documented, and adherence often declines over time, creating a tension between initial efficacy and long-term practicality.

C002.subject: Intermittent fasting
C002.object: short-term weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting short-term weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction]

[PATH:empirical] Head-to-head randomized controlled trial comparing time-restricted eating (e.g., 16:8) with daily calorie restriction over 12 months, including post-intervention follow-up — Directly tests the hypothesis in the relevant time domain and assesses whether short-term weight loss equivalence persists or diverges under longer observation.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of all randomized trials with ≥8-week interventions comparing intermittent fasting protocols to continuous calorie restriction, with subgroup analysis by intervention duration and adherence — Aggregates existing evidence to increase statistical power, assess heterogeneity, and identify potential moderators like protocol type or dropout rates.

[PATH:theoretical] Mechanistic study comparing hormonal and metabolic adaptations (e.g., insulin sensitivity, ghrelin, leptin, and resting energy expenditure) between intermittent fasting and continuous calorie restriction over 8–12 weeks — Tests the underlying premise that physiological responses might differ between the two regimens, which could explain or challenge the observed equivalence in weight loss.

qualifier.description: Multiple randomized controlled trials demonstrate similar reductions in body weight during the active intervention period, typically 8-24 weeks.

C004.subject: Intermittent fasting
C004.object: metabolic adaptations that undermine sustained weight loss beyond 12 months
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting metabolic adaptations that undermine sustained weight loss beyond 12 months]

[PATH:empirical] Long-term randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing alternate-day fasting vs. daily caloric restriction with objective metabolic hormone measurements (ghrelin, leptin, insulin) and body composition at 12, 18, 24 months — Directly tests the hypothesis by tracking hormonal adaptations and weight trajectory beyond 12 months, capturing the proposed biological-behavioral friction.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of intermittent fasting studies with ≥12-month follow-up, examining effect modification by compensatory eating behavior (e.g., post-fast caloric overshoot) — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether metabolic adaptation or behavioral rebound consistently undermines long-term weight loss, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled feeding study with fixed energy intake during alternate-day fasting to isolate metabolic compensation (e.g., reduced resting metabolic rate) from behavioral rebound — Distinguishes biological (hormonal/metabolic) from behavioral mechanisms, clarifying the primary driver of weight loss attenuation beyond 12 months.

qualifier.description: Alternate-day fasting patterns can trigger compensatory hormonal responses (e.g., increased ghrelin, reduced leptin) and behavioral rebound eating, potentially offsetting initial calorie deficits and creating a biological versus behavioral friction.

C005.subject: Adherence to intermittent fasting regimens
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Adherence to intermittent fasting regimens 6 to 12 months of practice]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort study tracking self-reported compliance, dropout, and weight outcomes in intermittent fasting participants at 0, 3, 6, 12, and 18 months — Directly measures adherence trajectories over the critical 6–12 month window, providing quantitative evidence whether stabilization or decline occurs.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing intermittent fasting to continuous calorie restriction, with subgroup analysis by duration (0–6 vs. 6–12 months) — Synthesizes existing data to detect overall patterns in adherence sustainability and identifies study-level moderators (e.g., diet type, support structure) that affect long-term compliance.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of behavioral maintenance using the Habit Formation and Self-Determination Theory frameworks, applied to intermittent fasting — Provides mechanistic predictions about when novelty effects wane and intrinsic motivation must replace external cues, generating testable hypotheses about adherence plateaus or declines around 6 months.

qualifier.description: Participant dropout rates increase and self-reported compliance decreases after the initial novelty phase, reducing the practical sustainability of the protocol.
